National Co-op Grocers includes 169 food co-ops operating 241 stores across 40 states and serving 1.3 million consumer owners. These are grocery stores, yes, but they are also community institutions. They're locally rooted, they're democratically accountable, they're connected to farmers and workers, to suppliers, consumers, and to community partners. And that's why food co-ops are relevant to the Sustainable Development Goals of zero hunger, decent work, reduced inequalities, responsible consumption and production, as well climate action. With regard to food access, NCG food co-ops accept SNAP, which is the Supplemental Nutrition Access Program, which is the major food assistance program in the U.S., and nearly two-thirds offer needs-based or other discounts, and more than half participate in fruit and vegetable incentive programs. In practical terms, this means food co-ops are not only selling food, but they're also helping make healthy food accessible to families who need it. When it comes to building local economies, food co-ops create markets for local farmers and producers. In NCG's 2025 Food Co-op Impact Survey, that data tells us that a quarter of food co-op sales come from local products. That's compared to just 2% at the average grocer. Because we are owned by our communities, we are accountable to those communities. We're more likely to ask, where does this food come from? Who produced it? Were they treated fairly? And does this purchase strengthen our local region? The average NCG Food Co-op works with an impressive 187 local suppliers. That's compared with just 41 at a traditional grocer. On equity and inclusion, co-ops are also using our purchasing power to support a more diverse economy. Last year, NCG Food Co-ops reported $63.5 million in inclusive trade sales. Those are products from businesses owned by people who have historically had barriers to the marketplace, including people of color, women, LGBTQ people, Women, veterans, and people with disabilities. NCG pledged to uphold the SDG to increase our support for smallholder and cooperative supply chains. And one way we have done so is through our partnership with the Federation of Southern Cooperatives, both through financial support as well as market infrastructure development and consulting, working to connect Black farmer co-ops in the southern U.S. To supply our NCG food co-ops. And on climate and responsible consumption, food co-ops are working to reduce waste, strengthen regional supply chains, supporting organic and fair trade products, and model more sustainable operations. In 2016, NCG committed to the SDG to offset our Scope 1 and Scope 2 carbon emissions annually at least through 2030, and to date we have upheld this commitment every single year. A good example of these things at work is the Briar Patch Food Co-op in California. Briar Patch is a community-owned grocery cooperative with two stores. In its recent impact reporting, Briar Patch noted that it has reached 100% renewable energy across both stores. It partnered with 188 local suppliers and farms, generating $5 million in local product sales. And it returned more than 200,000 pounds of food waste to local farms, closing the loop on their regional food system. Now that's local SDG in action. It's not abstract. It's a community-owned enterprise using everyday businesses decisions, whether it's purchasing, energy, employment, whether it's waste, finance, or governance, to produce broader public value. And this is not only about grocery stores. In the United States, there are more than 3— 30,000 cooperatives. Almost half of all Americans belong to a cooperative. The top 100 U.S. cooperatives generate more than $324 billion $1.5 trillion in annual sales. And this scale matters because it shows that cooperatives are not marginal. They are already a significant part of our economy. The opportunity is to recognize them more fully as partners in sustainable development. I want to connect this all to the theme of cooperatives for a peaceful world. Peace is not only the absence of conflict. It is also the presence of institutions that people trust. It is the presence of economic opportunity, democratic participation, social cohesion, and the ability of communities to solve problems together. Cooperatives build the kind of peace because they practice democracy in daily economic life. Members deliberate, they elect boards, they share benefits, and they make decisions not only as consumers or workers or producers but also as owners. And that makes cooperatives a pretty powerful model, but it does not make them perfect. And like all institutions, we must continue to improve, to become more inclusive, to meet the challenges of our time. But the model gives us a powerful start— starting point. People working together through democratic ownership to to meet common needs. And my closing message to you is that if we want the Sustainable Development Goals to move faster, if we want them to have lasting impact, governments and international institutions should treat cooperatives not only as stakeholders to consult, but as implementation partners. That means including cooperatives in national and local SDG strategies. It means supporting policies that help co-ops thrive. Whether it means designing procurement, financing, technical assistance, or policy frameworks that allow co-ops to do what they do best, to turn local ownership into practical solutions. The SDGs will not be achieved by policy alone. They'll be achieved through institutions and businesses that people trust, that they own, and that they use every day., and cooperatives are those institutions. Thank you.
